title: What Are The Benefits Of A SIP?
summary: A SIP is a standing instruction to invest a fixed amount in a mutual fund on a set date. See how units, NAV, kinds of SIP and dates work.
body_markdown:
## What is a SIP?


A SIP (systematic investment plan) is a standing instruction to invest a fixed amount in one mutual fund on a set date, usually every month. A mutual fund is a pool of money from many people, invested by a professional manager under SEBI rules. When you put money in, you get units. A unit is one small share of the fund's assets. The NAV (net asset value) is the price of one unit, worked out every day.


The idea that matters most is this: a SIP is a method, not a product. You do not buy "a SIP" the way you buy a fund. You buy a fund, and the SIP is how you pay for it, in instalments instead of all at once. Scheme documents list it as a facility of a scheme, and that is a fair way to think of it.


So everything about risk, return and tax belongs to the fund. The value of your SIP moves with the fund's NAV and can be lower than the amount you put in. SEBI makes every fund show a riskometer, a risk label on six levels from Low to Very High. That label describes the fund, not the SIP.


Two questions follow from this. A SIP has no interest rate; what you earn depends on the fund's NAV ([how the "rate" in a SIP works](https://koshex.com/blog/sip-interest-rate) ). And the risk is the fund's, not the SIP's ([whether a SIP is safe](https://koshex.com/blog/is-sip-safe) ).


## How does a SIP work, step by step?


You pick a fund, an amount, how often to invest and a date, and after that the money moves on its own each time. The sequence runs like this.


1. **Choose the fund, amount, frequency and date.** Dates, minimums and end dates are set in each scheme's documents and vary by fund house, so check the form.
2. **Complete KYC once.** KYC (know your customer) is the identity check you finish before your first investment.
3. **Set up a bank mandate.** A one-time mandate tells your bank it may pay the fund house up to a limit you set, each time you invest. One mandate can cover several SIPs, and it has to allow the largest instalment you plan, including any step-up. The detail is in our guide to the[one-time mandate](https://koshex.com/blog/one-time-mandate-otm-sip) .
4. **The money moves on the date.** Your SIP money goes from your bank account straight to the fund. A distributor such as Koshex never holds it, and the bank mandate is not in our name.
5. **Units are allotted.** The number of units is your amount divided by the NAV.


The NAV you get depends on when the money arrives. Your SIP buys units at the NAV of the day your money reaches the fund. That holds if it arrives by 3 pm on a business day, for funds other than liquid and overnight funds. Otherwise it gets the next business day's NAV. Our note on[cut-off timings](https://koshex.com/blog/mutual-fund-cut-off-timings-all-you-need-to-know) has more.


A tiny stamp duty is deducted from each purchase, so slightly fewer units are bought than the plain division gives. You get a confirmation by email or SMS within 5 working days of the request. A consolidated account statement follows by the 15th of the next month. It covers every month in which you had a transaction, SIP instalments included.


You don't need a demat account. Units can sit in a statement account, a record the fund house keeps of your units. A demat account is needed only if you want to trade units listed on a stock exchange. Our note on[whether you need a demat account](https://koshex.com/blog/do-we-need-a-demat-account-for-mutual-funds) has more.


### A worked example


Take ₹5,000 a month. The NAVs below are made-up figures, chosen to show the arithmetic.


Month NAV ₹5,000 buys


1 ₹100 50 units


2 ₹50 100 units


3 ₹100 50 units


Total 200 units for ₹15,000


Your average cost is ₹15,000 ÷ 200 units, which is ₹75 a unit. The simple average of the three NAVs is ₹83.33. The month with the low NAV bought the most units.


## What kinds of SIP can you choose?


Most SIPs are a fixed amount on a fixed date, and fund houses add variants that are set in each scheme's documents, not by SEBI. Here are the common ones.


**By frequency.** Daily, weekly, fortnightly, monthly and quarterly SIPs are all in use. Bi-monthly SIPs exist too. One scheme document sets a minimum of 6 instalments for daily to quarterly SIPs.


**Step-up or top-up.** The instalment rises by a fixed amount or a fixed percentage at set intervals. At one fund house, the interval is yearly or half-yearly. Our guide to the[step-up SIP](https://koshex.com/blog/step-up-sip) covers how it works.


**Several schemes on one form.** One fund house lets you register SIPs in up to five of its schemes on a single form.


**SIP cum SWP.** Here you run a SIP first, and SWP (systematic withdrawal plan) instalments, which take money out of the fund, start when the SIP's term ends. Our piece on[monthly income from mutual funds](https://koshex.com/blog/can-i-get-monthly-income-from-mutual-funds) looks at withdrawals.


**No end date.** If you give no end date, one fund house's form defaults to 40 years from the start date.


On Koshex, you can pause, cancel, change the amount or the date of, and step up a SIP.


## Which date should you choose for your SIP?


Choose a date a few days after your salary or other income arrives, so the money is in your account when the debit happens. The date is about cash flow, not returns.


One scheme document allows any date from the 1st to the 28th of the month for monthly and quarterly SIPs. If your date falls on a holiday, or on a day the month does not have, the instalment goes through on the next business day.


The date matters for a practical reason. If the account is short on the day, the debit fails and you buy no units that month. The[one-time mandate guide](https://koshex.com/blog/one-time-mandate-otm-sip) explains what happens after a failed debit.


## What does a SIP do for you, and what doesn't it do?


A SIP makes investing automatic and lets you start small, and it averages your cost per unit; it does not raise returns or remove risk.


**You can start small.** One scheme document takes a SIP from ₹100 and another asks for ₹200 a month. Each fund sets its own minimum.


**It builds a habit.** The money leaves on the date without you deciding each month. It suits investing out of a monthly salary.


**It smooths your average cost.** A SIP invests the same amount each time, so it buys more units when the NAV is low and fewer when it is high. The average cost per unit can never be higher than the simple average of the NAVs. That is all the method promises.


It does not promise a better result than a lump sum. A lump sum is a larger amount invested at one time. Say the NAV rises steadily from ₹50 to ₹75 to ₹100. ₹15,000 invested at ₹50 buys 300 units. ₹5,000 a month at ₹50, ₹75 and ₹100 buys 100 + 66.67 + 50, which is 216.67 units. The money invested earlier bought more. If you are weighing the two, read[SIP or lump sum: which is better](https://koshex.com/blog/when-is-the-right-time-to-invest-in-lump-sum-and-sip) .


**Growth can build on growth.** This is compounding: what the fund earns stays invested, so later growth is on a bigger amount. A SEBI-registered mutual fund's own income is exempt from tax, so trades inside the fund create no tax for you while you hold. Our article on[the power of compounding](https://koshex.com/blog/power-of-compounding-meaning-benefits-working) explains it, and the[SIP calculator](https://koshex.com/calculators/sip-calculator) lets you try numbers of your own.


A SIP also has limits.


- It pays no interest. The fund's NAV decides your result.
- It does not protect you from a fall in the NAV. Neither does a lump sum.
- It is not tax-free. Each instalment is taxed by the fund's rules when sold ([how SIP returns are taxed](https://koshex.com/blog/how-sip-returns-are-taxed) ).


## Can you stop a SIP or take your money out?


Yes, you can cancel a SIP at any time, and what you have invested stays in the fund until you sell it. Platforms that register SIPs must let you cancel active ones. Scheme documents say a SIP is cancelled within two business days of your request.


Stopping only ends future instalments. It sells nothing, so it carries no exit load, the fee some funds charge if you sell soon after buying. One fund house also offers a pause, after which the instalments restart on their own. Koshex customers can pause or cancel a SIP on Koshex. The full picture is in our guide to[stopping or pausing a SIP](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-stop-or-pause-a-sip) .


Selling is a separate step. Most funds have no lock-in, which is a period when you cannot sell at all.[ELSS funds](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/elss-funds) are funds you can claim as a tax deduction, up to a yearly limit. That is under section 123 (the old Section 80C), old tax regime only. They lock each instalment for three years from its own allotment date, the day those units are bought. The exit load cannot exceed 3% of the NAV. Because each instalment has its own purchase date, a load applies only to recent instalments still inside the fund's load period.


Sale proceeds normally reach your bank account within 3 working days. Read[how to sell mutual funds online](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-sell-mutual-funds-online-a-step-by-step-guide) before you do. If you hold an ELSS, see[what to do when the lock-in ends](https://koshex.com/blog/your-elss-lock-in-period-is-over-whats-next) .


## How do you start a SIP through Koshex?


Complete your KYC, then choose a fund and set the amount, frequency and date. On Koshex you invest in regular plans. A regular plan is the version of a fund bought through a distributor, here Koshex (AMFI registration ARN-154632), who helps you choose and stays with you afterwards.


As a distributor, Koshex helps you choose a fund that suits your goal and timeline. It reviews your holdings over time and flags changes, such as a fund's category, risk or ranking shifting. It talks you through sharp market falls before you redeem, that is, sell. And each financial year it helps with the ELSS and section 123 decision.


Browse the[mutual funds](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds) on Koshex, or read[how to invest in mutual funds online or offline](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-invest-in-mutual-funds-online-offline-in-india) . For the amount, see[how much to invest every month](https://koshex.com/blog/how-much-should-i-invest-in-mutual-funds-every-month) .
